title: Solomon's opening: all human affairs are empty
english: Thus says Solomon, son of David the king and prophet, to the whole Church of God—among all people the most honored king, and the wisest prophet. How empty and useless are all human affairs and pursuits, everything that belongs to human life. For no one can point to any benefit attached to these things that people, moving about the earth, are eager to accomplish with body and soul. They are defeated by temporal things, and they do not wish to see anything at all above the stars with the noble eye of the soul. Human life wears away day by day, through the cycles of hours and years and the fixed courses of the sun, as some things arrive and others slip away. The matter is like the passing of winter torrents that pour into the boundless deep of the sea with great turmoil. What God has established for human life remains fixed: being born from the earth, departing into the earth, the earth itself standing firm, the sun traveling around the whole earth and returning again to the same boundary, the winds likewise, and the rivers pouring into the sea—so many of them—and the winds that rush upon it, yet do not force it to overflow its limits, nor do they themselves transgress. These things that contribute to our life here have been fixed in this way. But the words and deeds devised by human beings have no measure. There is a great crowd of words, yet no benefit comes from this wandering idle talk. The human race is insatiable, both in speaking and in listening to another who speaks; and still more, it longs to gaze with idle eyes at everything that happens to come along. What could happen later that has not already been accomplished, or done by human beings? What new thing has not yet come to experience, that would be worth remembering? For I think there is nothing. Whatever someone might call recent or new, he will find upon reflection that it was not unknown even to the ancients. Just as former things are hidden in forgetfulness, so also present things will be dimmed in time for those who come after. And I am not improvising these things now as I address the Church; rather, having been entrusted with the kingdom of the Hebrews in Jerusalem, I have thought through all these things sufficiently.
